Michael Diamond and Seth Allcorn PHD

Dr Allcorn has 20 years of experience working with physicians, hospitals and academic medical centers. He has worked for 20 years as a part-time and full-time organizational consultant specializing in the management of change, strategic planning and organizational restructuring. Dr Allcorn is extensively published. He is the author or co-author of 10 books and over 60 papers that have appeared in scholarly and practitioner journals. He is a founding member of the International Society for the Psychoanalytic Study of Organizations.
containment (of conflicts and divisions); democracy (in the workplace); perversion; autistic-contiguous, paranoid-schizoid and depressive (modes of organizing experience)

Can democratic institutions contain conflict, division, and uncanny emotions with cultures of management that are frequently undemocratic? What distinguishes those institutions and organizations capable of containment from others? And, what are the psychodynamics at work in the perversion of democratic processes inside organizations? In this paper, we explore the psychodynamics of democracy in the workplace with a particular focus on unconscious and collusive forms of perverting democratic processes at work. We suggest that interpersonally and collectively the dialectical interplay between (1) autistic-contiguous, (2) paranoid-schizoid, and (3) depressive modes of experience and organized perceptions, which are necessary to the containment of divisions and conflicts in democratic organizations, is vulnerable to stress, anxiety, and psychological defenses that foster regression and collapse into more oppressive, authoritarian, and sadistic political cultures. With the objective of understanding perversions to democracy in the workplace, we find that a contemporary psychoanalytic view of organizations is more instructive than mainstream organization theory or that found in Foucault's writings on power and institutions.

Psychoanalysis has much to gain by incorporating ethnographic methods into its repertoire. Recent works in ethnographic psychoanalysis demonstrate how psychoanalysis stands to function better as both community intervention and participatory action research. This article describes the historical convergence between psychoanalysis and cultural anthropology and situates ethnographic psychoanalysis within interdisciplinary theory and practice.

Steven Groarke

Steven Groarke

80 Roehampton Lane, London SW15 5SL, UK
E-mail: s.groarke@roehampton.ac.uk

Steven Groarke  

Going Sane is not a book about psychoanalysis, but like all of Adam Phillips' books it tells us something about the current state of play of psychoanalysis. Thinking about what it would be like to be sane, what being sane might feel like for us today, Phillips reworks the initial Freudian principles of mind with reference to war. Far from a gratuitous reading of the history of psychoanalysis, Phillips' argument engages the very horizon of Freudian thought. He recounts a trajectory in Freud's own thinking where the polarity of pleasure and reality held good until, faced among other things with the phenomenon of repetitive traumatic dreams at the time of the First World War, Freud sought to account for our non-erotic aggression and hatred in terms of the death drive. The upheaval caused by the introduction of the latter remains part of Freud's difficult legacy: for the alternation of the pleasure principle and the reality principle, as Freud describes it, is incommensurable with his account of the conflict between Eros and death.

What does Phillips (1998) make of this difficulty? The short answer is that he refuses to settle for the pessimistic hypothesis of the death drive. In The Beast in the Nursery, he already takes issue with the idea that a person's life is a war between life and death instincts. The present book augments this line of thinking by reworking Freud's ideas of pleasure and reality as a composite principle of sane kindness. On this reading, sanity is neither the alternative of madness nor a synonym of reality. Instead, Phillips describes a relationship of forces in which the gratification of our libidinous and aggressive impulses is coupled with the aspiration of kindness. Whereas Freud emphasizes the internalization of parental prohibitions and demands, Phillips ventures beyond the theme of interdiction in search of “a new story about kindness” (2005, p 238). The book envisages the sane life beyond the “humiliating morality” of our sense of goodness (2005, p 239). This may be asking more of psychoanalysis than it is capable of providing, namely, an interpretation of the grounds rather than the genesis of ethical subjectivity. Nevertheless, Phillips is adamant that sanity should embody our best efforts to avoid humiliating ourselves and others. As such, sanity may be understood as a principle of mental functioning, if not a worldview. To state the argument in bald terms: even if society must be defended (and Phillips is in no doubt about our needing protection), the sane self also has to answer for war on the grounds of kindness.

Sheila Namir  

Psychoanalysis and Women, The Annual of Psychoanalysis from the Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis and the Chicago Psychoanalytic Society, contains some exciting and historically interesting papers and contributions by some of the stellar theorists and clinicians in the field. The volume is divided into four sections with the first two comprised of clinical and theoretical papers on the psychology of women and the latter two including personal narratives and historical/biographical pieces about a few of the women who shaped psychoanalysis. In their introduction, the editors state that “no aspect of psychoanalytic theory has been, since the early years of the field, more problematical than the psychology of women” (p 1). Their effort is to represent the revolution that has taken place since the 1960s, when basic questions about the psychology of women began to be rethought from a woman's point of view (p 5). Despite the editors' aspirations, however, the questions that are addressed by this volume seem unusually narrow and, particularly in the theoretical section, the papers return us to an earlier “troubled and problematical” moment when the emphasis was on femininity, passivity and masochism in women.

Variations on the theme of femininity and passivity are presented by Jessica Benjamin, Julia Kristeva, Christine Kieffer and Ethel Person. Benjamin continues her exciting work on complementarity focusing on the active-passive opposition as templates for masculine and feminine psychic life. Noting that femininity is partially constructed by the male psyche to contain excess tension and anxiety in the female body, she argues against women being passive containers and men being the active owners of erotic energy. Her thinking about the possibilities of “owning desire” and holding passivity as part of the surrender to a process of mutual recognition redeems “passivity” from the traumatic realm as well as from gender complementarity. Kristeva revisits and deconstructs female sexuality by renaming the phallic phase as the “primary oedipal phase,” which is both passive and implicated in “interactive subjectivity” (p 61). Describing the ambiguities that exist for females in the primary and secondary oedipal phases, she distinguishes between female and femininity, and she attributes psychic depth and maturity to the female who “manages to accomplish the complex tourniquet imposed on her by the primary and secondary oedipal phases” (p 66). Kieffer addresses the father-daughter relationship from a self-psychological point of view, attempting to integrate Benjamin's work with self-psychology via the conventional view of the female “oedipal victory.” Her analysis of the problems faced by the female oedipal victor eerily echoes theorizing about “masculine women” that was prevalent in Freud's day. What Kieffer adds is only the possibility for “false recognition” by the father, which results in the daughter's serving as his narcissistic extension. Finally, Person provides a culturalist point of view as she continues her work on “authentic power” (Person, 2002) and the “cultural unconscious.

Will Stockton

Will Stockton

Bloomington

Will Stockton  

“It seems that if Freud did not exist we would have to invent him” (p 7). This is the Voltairian wager of Jerry Aline Flieger's Is Oedipus Online?, one of six books published so far in The MIT Press's promising new series Short Circuits. Series editor Slavoj Žižek explains that through the “privileged instrument” of Lacanian psychoanalysis, Short Circuits “intends to revive a practice of reading which confronts a classic text, author, or notion with its own hidden presumptions, and thus reveals its disavowed truth” (pp ix, x). In Oedipus, Flieger does just this by confronting cyber theory and nonlinear science with their disavowed Freudian foundations. Her wager pays off handsomely. Claims of Freud's death, she demonstrates, are premature: he is alive and well, online and surfing through the millennial field.

Surfing with him is Oedipus, no longer the harbinger of the familial complex that produces individual subjects, but rather a search engine in the intersubjective cyberspace of knowledge and desire - a paradigm of “rotational site or differential position” (p 58). After the hits that Oedipus has taken over the past few decades, especially in the fields of gender and queer studies, Flieger's defense is daring, and it warrants multiple evidentiary approaches or “sitings”. In Chapter 2 (a chapter that also constitutes an extended response to Žižek's own flirtation with the possibility of Oedipus' dissolution in cyberspace), Flieger sits Oedipus within Abbott and Costello's Who's on First? routine, which comically collapses name and base position, and Lacan's Schema L, which graphs the quadrilateral relation between the barred subject, the object of desire, the ego ideal, and the Other. Focusing on the play of positions, the ability of subjects to move between positions in a symbolic field, Flieger frees Oedipus from his culturally specific moorings to make him our contemporary. Like Oedipus, she argues, we postmoderns are wracked with insecurities about our own identity; we wonder whether others are who they say they are, and where the human ends and the inhuman begins. The Internet, space exploration, neuroscience, genetic engineering, and xenophobic conspiracy theories have in fact compounded these insecurities, providing new fields in which to perceive that subjectivity is always an effect of the spatial relation between self, other, and Other, the core Oedipal triangulation.

David Marriott

1116 High Street

David Marriott  

Bergner's task in Taboo Subjects is to urge a “political” reading of psychoanalysis in the wake of race and to show how race and gender/sex intersect. In this strategic enterprise elaborated, for the most part, through a thematic (and not a particularly formal) approach to African-American literary texts, there is often an uneasy struggle between models and history, between theoretical speculation and textual analysis, and this struggle is never quite resolved.

Her first chapter, which locates a gender bias in Fanon's reading of Mayotte Cápecia's Je suis Martiniquaise, is typical of this unease. Instead of addressing how race complicates Fanon's psychoanalysis of female sexuality, Bergner's reading turns to history and Cápecia's socio-economic position - as if her work as a laundress was any kind of answer to what Fanon sees as the troubling connection between “lactification” and negrophobia in her work. This reading, in my view, fails to address Fanon's reading of phobia as a structure of racist society, one that returns as a symptom marking Cápecia's aggression towards black men (and women) and her own sexual and symbolic investiture in whiteness. What is most troubling is the absence of any consideration of Cápecia's own affective ambivalence to black women: that ambivalence suggests a relation between sexuality and phobia in which the “epidermalization” of inferiority is used to mark lighter from darker subjects regardless of gender. Such a reading would have rendered Bergner's accusation of a gender bias in Fanon more dialectical and just.

The strategy adopted in other chapters also involves the use of analogical methods that are never openly addressed as such. The strategy might be described as one of implication, but the homologies are often too hasty, at least methodologically. For example, Douglass’ witnessing of his aunt being whipped in the 1845 Narrative is like the boy's oedipal witnessing of a primal scene. Here, at the level of perception, what tends to fall out of view is any notion of the “gaze” (Lacan), or any nuanced sense of visuality. These analogies produce further equations (and further confusions): the mulatto body is the “traumatic kernel” of the racial symbolic resisting symbolization, symbolic integration, etc. (p 56), but isn't this body clearly symbolized and symbolically integrated? Moreover, what does it mean to say that miscegenation occupies the place of Lacan's “real”? I think this association requires more working out than the concept of “ideological fantasy” permits.

Aggressive and other powerful affective forces pose a real challenge for the project of a pluralist democracy. The danger is that new deliberative techniques are adopted which facilitate inclusiveness and manageability, but at the expense of impassioned argument. This paper examines the Listening Post, a deliberative technique, which has specifically emerged out of the therapeutic culture and which therefore foregrounds the role of unconscious affect in group communication. This article provides a case study of an event that drew upon free associational methods for promoting ‘reflexive citizenship’. The case study highlights some of the difficulties in distinguishing between ‘cool’ and ‘hot’ forms of connectivity, between impassioned argument and a ‘fight to the death’ and between forms of communicative action which simulate the reflexive exploration of difference and those which facilitate the real thing.

The absolute state of mind refers to a core disposition in society and the individual. In society, it is clearest in religious, especially fanatical, fundamentalism; in the individual, in a narcissistic fundamentalism described by post-Kleinians as pathological narcissistic structures. Historians and sociologists also see normal and rational strategy in a range of fundamentalist groups, and for psychoanalysts, pathological narcissistic structures are extremes also found in ordinary people. My aim is to draw on recent scholarship to extract a core theme - the absolute state of mind - that characterizes this fundamentalist disposition in its extremism and its rationality, and to describe it psychoanalytically.

This essay continues the exploration of Freud's “exigency and going-astray,” as they are defined in Jean Laplanche's essay of that name, by tracing one major going-astray detected by Laplanche in Freud's thinking: Freud's erasure of his own radical discovery that the other is central to the self. In the process of restoring the Freudian model of the decentered self, Laplanche creates the theoretical category of the message, or the enigmatic signifier. I argue that Laplanche's model of the enigmatic signifier can be extended past childhood to illuminate the signifying processes of adult citizens forced to deal with enigmatic messages from the state. By way of example, I use the notion of the enigmatic signifier to analyze the US public's long-sustained patient acceptance of George W Bush's misleading rhetoric.

The Revolt of the Primitive: an Inquiry into the Roots of Political Correctness examines contradictions and injustices in the exercise of political correctness, primarily in educational institutions. Schwartz's dissent from political correctness derives from a psychoanalytic reading of what the demands for political correctness represent: the giving over of the self and group to the primordial or primitive maternal. What results is the emasculation of the Father, the appearance of social policies and groups dominated by the maternal ego ideal, and the disappearance of respect generated by the imagery and practices of authority. This is particularly the case in Universities where traditional authority has been supplanted by the values of political correctness, and in a set of public assumptions about behavior that psychoanalytically “expresses the premise of the primordial mother whose children have no need, and certainly no right, to have their own minds” (p 155). In this view, political correctness is an assault on paternal law, on rationality, and on balance in the institution. Further, it is an attack on moderation and fairness; it replaces guilt with shame, and demonstrates extreme impatience with the ambivalence and doubt associated with the superego.

In this meticulously argued, lucid and well-written book, Schwartz does present some interesting theoretical ideas and questions: I found his use of the concept of projective identification as a way of describing group reactions to abhorrent values to be useful. We often hate others to avoid hating ourselves; and there is no reason to think such a mechanism does not condition strident ideological attacks coming from both left and right on University campuses. The notion that the world holds us like the primordial mother (p 132) - “our desire to deny the world outside ourselves and what that world tells us about our own limitations” (p 111) - gives us fascinating insight into the sense of entitlement, narcissism, and the range of feeling behind entitlement demands. For Schwartz this sense of being contained and held by righteousness leads often to intolerance and an unwillingness to subordinate individual feeling to a rational construct that seeks fairness.

People think psychoanalysts are smart. Beyond their supposed insight into the mysteries of human behavior, psychoanalysts often seem to have an impressive range of knowledge. It's not hard to think of images of psychoanalytic intelligence: Freud's broad humanistic learning is familiar to all, and Bruce Fink's introductions to the selected and full Écrits close with a note about the impossibility of keeping up with Lacan's myriad references. In our own time, Elisabeth Young-Bruehl, Juliet Mitchell, Jonathan Lear, and Adam Phillips all spring effortlessly to mind as exemplary psychoanalytic intellectuals, moving with apparent effortlessness from clinical vignette to literary or philosophical discourse to metapsychological reduction. And then there's Žižek….

People think psychoanalysts are stupid, or, if not stupid, then deluded, vain charlatans: Outmoded by innovations in pharmacology, committed to phallogocentric logic if not outright misogyny, superceded by 12-step groups, and just a little too Edwardian for a wired world. And, again, it's not hard to think of examples: Frederick Crews, François Roustang, and Alan Sokal all come quickly to mind in the camp of those who find analysts stupid - not to mention HMOs all across the United States. Psychoanalysts themselves frequently treat each other as both smart and stupid: It's not clear whether it's less edifying to hear someone newly excited by Lacan rail against the IPA, or someone who's never read Lacan declaim against the “short session”.

This is an ambitious book with a title that beckons us and promises much, particularly given the current political climate in the United States. In response to the terrorism of September 11, 2001, the United States has become involved in two wars against oppressive regimes, one directly related in Afghanistan and the other unrelated in Iraq, and President Bush has articulated an aggressive policy of bringing freedom and democracy to the Middle East. At the same time, freedom, in terms of civil liberties, has been sorely tried by the Bush administration, from apparently illegal federal wiretapping of citizens to imprisonment of suspected terrorists or suspicious immigrants who are denied access to lawyers or judicial process, to the torture of detainees. Yet, Bush was re-elected when much of this was known. A recent survey of one thousand Americans found that only one in four could name more than one of the five fundamental First Amendment freedoms: speech, religion, press, assembly, and petition to redress of grievances (McCormick Tribune Freedom Museum, 2006). The question posed by these circumstances is whether this country, when threatened from without, can maintain its tradition of freedom. Thus, a book with this title seems particularly appropriate at this time.

However, Alford is not writing about political freedom per se. In fact, he does not define what he means by “freedom”. Instead, he attempts to find out what his American informants mean when they use the word “freedom”, and hopes that by doing so he will go to the heart of how Americans think about freedom. To do so, he obtained a “non-random” sample, which one must turn to the research appendix in the book to understand. Most, he says, came from the state university where he was employed, 35 between the ages of 18 and 30, and 17 between the ages of 31 and 74.

Miriam Dixson  

If our species is not actually hooked on domination, history shows that we repeatedly engage with its manifestations, weaving them into emotional textures at the deepest levels. Isaac Balbus's Mourning and Modernity asks what emotional hold domination might exercise over us. By exploring that hold, how might we weaken domination in its specifically modern forms?

As one of America's leading critical social and political theorists, over two decades Balbus has developed a neo-Kleinian, feminist account of sexual, political and technological domination. His views have elicited Marxist, non-psychoanalytic feminist and post-structural criticisms, and in the first half of this book, Balbus replies to them. The second half applies his psychoanalytically informed theory of cultural mourning to a number of salient topics, among them Marxism, the 1960s counterculture, reparations for racism and the contradictions of high technology. Mourning and Modernity is masterful, passionate, tightly argued, warily hopeful. It draws primarily on Melanie Klein's key concepts (splitting, integration, mourning, reparation), but beyond these, also on Balbus's original theorizing. The book thus renews the tradition of critical cultural psychoanalysis that includes Herbert Marcuse, Christopher Lasch, Dorothy Dinnerstein and Joel Whitebook.

Vital to Balbus's argument is a stunning and provocative hypothesis about the foundations of domination. It links infancy, parenting and splitting as a basic cognitive/emotional mental mechanism. The forms of domination that most bedevil us today, the writer contends, are “emotionally anchored in different forms of mother-dominated child rearing” (p xi). Elaborating this, Balbus critically deploys the insights of a landmark feminist text, The Mermaid and the Minotaur, published in 1976 by the feminist “mothering” theorist Dorothy Dinnerstein. Trained as a cognitive psychologist but profoundly influenced by Freud and Klein, Dinnerstein drew on universal, transhistorical myths which testify to the profoundly ambivalent feelings about women held by men and women alike: they testify to unbounded worshipful adoration, to fear, hate and envy without limit.

Communities that have experienced public traumas often must contend with well-intentioned but unhelpful responses from outsiders. How they manage this task conveys a great deal about their particular histories and their current struggles. Three-person psychoanalysis and contemporary psychoanalytic ethnography both acknowledge that misrecognition necessarily inheres in even the most diligent empathic efforts. Work that draws on the contributions of these theories may help communities understand and survive the effects of empathic failure in the wake of trauma. A research trip to Jasper, Texas, site of the racially motivated murder of James Byrd, Jr, is described to illustrate these ideas.

Frédéric Declercq   Assistant Professor at the Department of Psychoanalysis and Consulting Psychology at the University of Ghent, where he teaches psychodiagnostics, sexuality and sexual disturbances, and models in psychoanalysis from a Freudian-Lacanian point of view. He is in private psychoanalytical practise and is also a forensic expert.
capitalist discourse; social bonds; jouissance; libidinal enjoyment; Freud; Lacan; Marx

Drawing together Lacan's statements about capitalist discourse, the author argues that it carries anti-social effects and brings about a regime that, in the end, revolves around a lack of libidinal enjoyment. The capitalist discourse would have an anti-social nature because it does not connect subjects to other subjects but entails connecting subjects to objects of libidinal enjoyment. However, the libidinal bond with the object appears to be deceitful because, in the end, the capitalist discourse installs a regime that is characterized by lack-of-enjoyment. Moreover, the subject can no longer be considered to occupy the position of an agent. In a capitalist discourse, it is not the subject that is in charge any more, but the libidinal object. Put differently, the subject is not exploited by the capitalist anymore, but by the objects of libidinal enjoyment. This will lead Lacan to say that, in a capitalist discourse, everybody is a proletarian.

Accoyer, Jacques-Alain Miller, Žižek, psychologization, politics

Pseudo-activity was Žižek's harsh judgment of JA Miller, who led the opposition against the French amendment Accoyer. Is the French “furor agitandi”, which denounces out loud what they see as “Lacanian-bashing”, a fight in the wrong arena? The buzz indeed seems to serve to cover up the socio-political dimension, and this becomes clear when one discerns the social forces that lie behind the amendment: psychologization and psychiatrization, the perfect partners of post-politics. What threatens psychoanalysis is not an anti-psychological discourse, but on the contrary psychological discourse as such. The French resistance seems to have missed this political appointment with its Golem. This leads to the question: do the current events point to another missed moment, that of Freud missing the political meeting with modernity?

Projective Identification as a Defense Mechanism When Facing the Threat of an Ecological Hazard

Smadar Ben-Asher and Nurit Goren MSW

Nurit Goren

Tzivoni 18, Lehavim, Israel
E-mail: nurit@interpage.co.il

Tzivoni 18, Lehavim, Israel

Nurit Goren   Psychotherapist, Group Analyst, and Staff Member in the “Conducting Groups Program”, Tel Aviv University. Also a course convener of the “Introduction to Group Analysis” and member in Israeli Institute of Group Analysis (I.I.G.A.) and Innovation and Changes in Society (I.C.S.).
projective identification; parent/soldier-sons relations; ecological hazard; cancer

The article examines the psychological use of projective identification to deal with the threat inherent in a severe ecological hazard. When information was uncovered regarding the high incidence of cancer diagnosed among Israeli soldiers who trained in a polluted river during their military service in an elite commando unit, a group of parents came together to demand that the state take responsibility for the sick soldiers. In contrast, their soldier-sons preferred to continue identifying with the army's position, which denied the connection between cancer and training in the polluted river. We argue that when fear arises for the lives of the soldier-sons they project their unbearable parts into their parents, who hold their projected parts and take concrete action, and relieve them of the struggle between the pole of life and the pole of death. The process ends when the state finally acknowledges its responsibility for the soldiers, thus enabling transformation.

unconscious; dichotomous reasoning; normative unconscious; historical contingency; psychosocial

Debates around issues of free will and determinism continue unabated and appear to be no nearer to a resolution. This article focuses on a recent paper by Lynne Layton to show how dichotomous reasoning can lead to positionality and thereby to a closing-off of possibilities rather than towards a resolution of this debate. Taking the transferential encounter as an example, the author questions current thinking on the so-called “unbridgeable gap” between unconscious drives and the social world and suggests that if psychosocial approaches are to work they have to be able to hold on to the idea of a universal unconscious and to be able to reconcile this with the structures of social existence into which agents are born and live out their lives.

Roland Végső   Doctoral candidate at the English Department of the State University of New York, Buffalo, where he is a member of the Center for the Study of Psychoanalysis and Culture and an editor of Umbr(a): A Journal of the Unconscious.
psychoanalysis and religion; the messianic; the prophetic; community; frustration

Contemporary theoretical interest in the intersections of politics and religion led to the redefinition of the category of the messianic as an inherent category of human subjectivity. In my paper, however, I argue that through a re-examination of Freud's work on the concept of frustration, we can conclude that psychoanalysis falls within the register of the prophetic rather than that of the messianic. The prophetic emerges here as the injunction to realize the community in the living present in accordance with the law that instituted the community in the first place.

In this position paper, we explore psychoanalytic and psycho-social interventions in communities. We start by looking at some of the historical developments in the United Kingdom of psychoanalytically informed professional practice and the way in which various strategies have developed for taking psychoanalysis into the community. We then go on to examine contemporary examples of this work in Bulgaria and South Africa, which the authors of this paper are involved in; these interweave with themes around HIV/AIDS, gender, masculinity, class and ethnicity. We conclude by offering some reflections about the relationship between psychoanalysis, practice and community intervention in which we ask a set of critical questions that we hope will stimulate debate.

The Social Significance of Synchronicity

Roderick Main PHD

Roderick Main

Wivenhoe Park, Colchester CO4 3SQ, UK

Roderick Main   Lecturer in Psychoanalytic Studies at the University of Essex and the author of The Rupture of Time: Synchronicity and Jung's Critique of Modern Western Culture (Brunner-Routledge, 2004).
Jung; analytical psychology; modernity; mass society; synchronicity

This paper aims to contribute to a reassessment of the social significance of C.G. Jung's (1875-1961) analytical psychology. Contrary to a tenacious perception that Jung's work is little concerned with society, this paper suggests that the social dimension is a concern that permeates all of Jung's work, even his apparently most esoteric. The paper looks first at Jung's diagnosis of the problem of modernity, next at his understanding and general analytical psychological critique of mass society, and then at the contribution of his concept of synchronicity (meaningful acausal connection) to this critique. It concludes with a brief reflection on the possible usefulness of synchronicity for illuminating contemporary social and cultural events.

Ricardo Ainslie

Ricardo Ainslie  

In the summer of 1998, three white men dragged James Byrd Jr, a 46-year-old unemployed African-American man, to his death in Jasper, Texas. The murder quickly drew national and international attention as a “modern day lynching”. The brutality of the crime (Byrd had been chained by the ankles and dragged for three miles behind a pickup truck), and the racial hatred reflected in it (two of the men eventually convicted of the murder were members of a White supremacist gang which they had joined while in prison and a cache of racist material was discovered in the apartment shared by the men), shocked the nation. The murder also created an immediate sense of crisis within Jasper itself. There were rampant rumors within this remote, East Texas community of 8,000 inhabitants that the murder was perhaps part of a broader Ku Klux Klan conspiracy. Many African Americans were fearful of leaving their homes. Many whites feared that the racial themes that defined the murder, some of whose details conformed with a well-known lynching that had taken place in the neighboring county in the 1920s when an African-American victim had been tied to the back of a pickup truck and dragged around the courthouse before being hanged in front of his house, might result in reprisals against whites.

This essay presents an explicit outline of almost everything that has implicitly governed Laplanche's methodological purpose over the last 30 odd years. Of particular interest in the essay are the following: a critique of Jung and Ricoeur, together with a clear exposition of what impels Laplanche's emphatically anti-hermeneutic approach to Freud; the suggestion of points of continuity between Laplanche's early collaborative publications (with Leclaire and Pontalis) and his subsequent solo work; an account of the singularity of Freud's analytic method and its implications for a textual analysis of Freud; the broaching of the notion of the “exigency” (exigence) of Freud's thought, and its relation to desire.

His most recent major works to be translated into English are Essays on Otherness and The Unconscious and the Id. Professor Laplanche is also scientific director of the ongoing project to translate Freud's Oeuvres Complètes.
Freud; hermeneutics; interpretation; the other

In this piece, Laplanche returns to and develops the insights of the earlier “Interpreting” essay. He goes on to give a striking re-elaboration of the idea of “exigency” in terms of his own reformulation of Freudian drive theory, arguing that evolution of Freud's thought is constrained and driven (poussé) to re-enact the evolution of the object it thinks: the narcissistic closure of the human psyche. In this connection Laplanche also introduces the related notion of theoretical “goings astray” (fourvoiements) - the extensive coverings-over of the radical Copernican essence of Freud's own discovery, which the exigency of his thought has brought about. As such, this second piece sets out two concepts which, for Laplanche, define the major discursive axes of Freud's oeuvre and thus orient the critical exposition of Freud which is so crucial to Laplanche's own theoretical work.

transference, countertransference (bodily), body modifications, relational psychoanalysis, self-cutting, cosmetic surgery, tattooing

The materiality of the body in a culture of mind (clinical psychoanalysis) offers perspectives on inside/outside and body/mind continuums. Presenting two examples, one from the perspective of an analyst and the other from the perspective of an analysand, I explore the effects of body modifications (self-cutting, tattooing and cosmetic surgery) on the relational matrix when the focus on the surface of the body immobilizes the fluidity of these continua. Presenting clinical issues of embodiment/disembodiment, I offer a relational psychoanalytic view of the bodymind in treatment.

(I Can't Get No) Enjoyment: Lacanian Theory and the Analysis of Nationalism

Yannis Stavrakakis and Nikos Chrysoloras

Nikos Chrysoloras

Wivenhoe Park, Colchester CO4 3SQ, UK
E-mail: yanstavr@yahoo.co.uk

London, UK

Nikos Chrysoloras   Studied International Relations at the University of Wales, Aberystwyth, and Political Theory at the University of Essex. He is currently reading for a PhD at the Department of Government and the Hellenic Observatory of the London School of Economics and Political Science. The title of his PhD thesis is “Religion and Nationalism in Greek and Greek-Cypriot Political Culture”. He has published articles on religion and the nation in contemporary Greece.
Lacan; nationalism; juissance; identification; discourse

This article explores the potential of Lacanian theory to improve our understanding of nationalism. Undoubtedly, constructionist and modernist approaches have been instrumental in explaining the (modern) emergence of nationalism. However, important as these approaches to nationalism may be, they tend to emphasize the form of nationalist discourses, rather than their force. They can explain the modes of their articulation and highlight their historicity and contingency, but cannot sufficiently account for their weight, salience and longevity. The Lacanian concept of enjoyment (juissance), on the other hand, offers an analytical angle able to explain the remarkable stability and force of national identifications within the milieu of modernity. We conclude that, developing further certain Freudian insights, Lacanian psychoanalysis can be an essential resource in efforts to construct a more comprehensive theory of nationalism.

341 Education South, Edmonton, Alberta, Canada T6G 2G5

Jan Jagodzinski  

Lacan; video games; interactivity; interpassivity; violence

This essay explores video game cybersubjects and the myths surrounding video game violence and its addiction, made possible through new forms of interactive media. Three psychic structures - psychotic, obsessive and hysterical - are developed to better grasp why a moral “panic” has emerged concerning these games. I develop the concept of “interpassivity” to further our understanding of why the addictive potential of video games continues to make them controversial.

Jacques China

Jacques China

54 Compton Road, London N1 2PB, UK

Jacques China   Psychoanalyst in private practice and in the National Health Service. He is founder member of The College of Psychoanalysts - UK and its first President. His former background is in academic and research psychology at University College, London, UK. His interest is in the scientific validation of psychoanalysis, and he is now concerned with the foundation of a new academic College of Psychoanalysis and the development there of a programme for a professional doctorate in psychoanalysis.
state regulation; statutory regulation; UK; international

This is a review of the international conference on Psychoanalysis and State Regulation organized by The College of Psychoanalysts - UK. I summarize the background leading to the conference and review presentations by psychoanalysts from several other countries about the relationship between psychoanalysis and the state in their countries. There follows a brief description of the key issues considered in parallel workshops during the course of the conference, and a review of those papers at the conference that gave rise to the greatest degree of controversy. Finally, I review the two plenary sessions and the issues raised there, together with an overall view of the outcome of the conference.
